content:
Q: I do quite a bit of walking in Williams Nature Center. I get a little bored with going on the same trails and have seen where visitors have made their own trails through the park.

I’m wondering if there are any plans to add trails to the center. They don’t have to be paved. Wood chips would be fine.

A: For people not familiar with Williams Nature Center, it’s a Blue Earth County Park on the north side of Highway 68 just east of Minneopa State Park. The park is particularly nice for people with mobility issues, because the trails are flat and paved. And the park has a pair of spectacular overlooks that are especially impressive this time of year when fall colors are peaking. One overlook provides a view of the Minnesota River Valley and the other faces both the river valley and the gorge that carries Minneopa Creek down to the Minnesota River.

As for the reader’s desire for more trail variety, Blue Earth County Public Works Director Ryan Thilges said that won’t be happening anytime soon.

“Thank you for reaching out. Currently, we do not have plans to add additional trails at Williams Nature Center, whether paved or wood-chipped,” Thilges said. “We do, however, have some work planned at the Nature Center focused on restoring and improving the natural habitat.”

The boost to the ecosystem comes as the park approaches its 50th birthday. Williams Nature Center was created in the 1980s from land donated by the Tulsa-based energy firm Williams Companies.

“Through a partnership with Great River Greening, we will be working on oak savanna restoration, including controlling invasive woody vegetation such as buckthorn and planting native vegetation,” Thilges said. “We’re hopeful this work will help improve the overall quality of the park and the experience for visitors.”

The question got Ask Us Guy thinking about the reader’s desire for new trails to explore. With fall color season arriving, maybe it’s time to put together a list of some of the best options.

Send in your favorite local spots for nature walks, along with a brief description of what makes them worth visiting, and we’ll run the suggestions in an Ask Us column in a couple of weeks.

Here are a couple to start.

Like Williams, Minneopa State Park has a trail that features the Minneopa Creek gorge. The trail starts at the park’s picnic grounds, on the Bison Range side of Minneopa, and gradually takes hikers along the edge and into the deep ravine, ending where the creek empties into the Minnesota River.

For people who like no-fee options like Williams Nature Center, Mankato’s Rasmussen Woods nature park is another good choice. To see the entire park, there’s an entrance to Rasmussen near the intersection of Oak Knoll Road and Park View Avenue in west Mankato. Follow the trail to the Nature Center’s main parking area off of Rasmussen Road and keep going south and west all the way to the trail’s end beneath the Red Jacket/West Mankato Trail.

The walk provides forests, dolomite rock formations and a marsh before it reaches the bike trail. Go below the trestle and circle up to the bike trail, following it north to Moreland Avenue. Head east on Moreland, and you’ll be back to your Oak Knoll starting point after four or five blocks of neighborhood walking.

Q: Every night around 10 pm, what appears to be a fairly large drone with red lights flies over the upper North Mankato bluffs from north to south.

Any ideas on what it might be?

A: Ask Us Guy has been doing this column for quite a few years, and he finally gets his first UFO question. And it came right as he was about to suggest a scenic hike through the woods, prairie and ridgelines of North Mankato’s beautiful Bluff Park. Imagine his embarrassment if readers had taken the advice only to suffer an alien abduction and all of the unpleasant probing that reported comes with those experiences.

Not having either Mulder’s number or Scully’s, he called April Larson, communications and outreach coordinator for the city of North Mankato, hoping there was a mundane municipal explanation for the drone-like flier.

“This is not a city drone,” Larson said. “Checking with various departments, no staff were aware of this specific one. Thank you for inquiring!”

So, OK, here’s another one where readers are going have to pitch in.

If you’ve seen this unidentified aerial phenomenon or are the person/intelligence agency/alien species behind its appearance, contact Ask Us at The Free Press, 418 S. Second St., Mankato, MN 56001. Call Mark Fischenich at 344-6321 or email your question to mfischenich@mankatofreepress.com; put “The Truth is Out There” in the subject line.
